paragraph.text: I13. "Without zoos, several species would already be extinct"

the argument has real cases on its side. The Arabian oryx, Przewalski's horse, the California condor and the scimitar-horned oryx disappeared, or nearly disappeared, from the wild and only came back because there were individuals in captivity. But captive breeding was decisive for a small share of recovered species: according to a survey published in

and later revised, it was a major action for 13 of the 68 vertebrate species that moved out of threatened categories. Most conservation comes from protecting habitats. And reintroduction programs involve a small fraction of the animals kept in zoos, nearly all of whom are displayed to the public and never return to the wild.

"If it weren't for zoos, lots of animals would have vanished already. Many species only exist today because someone kept a few in captivity and released them later."
Several species became extinct in the wild and survived only in captivity.
Captive breeding made it possible to reintroduce some of these species.
Without institutions that keep animals in captivity, these species would have disappeared.
So zoos are necessary, and keeping animals in them is justified.

P1, P2 and P3 are true for some cases. The conclusion overgeneralizes: it justifies breeding for conservation where it's needed, not the display of thousands of animals from species that aren't threatened.
fails in the step from "some programs saved species" to "zoos in general are justified".
"Without zoos, lots of animals would be extinct by now."
"Most species that recovered were saved in captivity."
"We take part in international breeding programs for threatened species."
"Ex situ conservation is a safety net against extinction."
"Zoos conserve species and educate." (which is I12)

Some species almost disappeared, and were only saved because people looked after a few animals and then released them into the wild. That's wonderful. But most animals in zoos aren't threatened and will never go back to the wild. And the best way to save animals is to look after the forests and grasslands where they live.

There are real cases: the Arabian oryx, Przewalski's horse, the California condor and the scimitar-horned oryx were saved thanks to individuals in captivity. But they aren't the majority: captive breeding was a major action for 13 of the 68 vertebrate species that moved out of threatened categories, and most conservation comes from protecting habitats. Reintroduction programs involve a small fraction of zoo animals. Breeding a threatened species to return it to the wild is different from keeping thousands of animals on display.
"How many of the animals in this zoo will ever go back to the wild?"
They're few, and almost always come with habitat protection
Captive breeding helped in some cases
It was a major action for 13 of 68 recovered species
Breeding for conservation can be necessary
Displaying non-threatened animals isn't justified by that

The Arabian oryx became extinct in the wild in 1972 and was reintroduced in Oman from 1982. Every remaining wild California condor was captured in 1987, and the species returned to the wild in 1992. The scimitar-horned oryx, declared extinct in the wild in 2000, was reintroduced in Chad from 2016 and reclassified as "Endangered" in 2023.

in 2011 identified captive breeding as a major action in the recovery of 13 of the 68 vertebrate species whose extinction risk fell, a figure revised by the authors themselves after it was challenged. Most recoveries came from protecting habitats, fighting poaching and controlling invasive species.
The same study shows that zoos keep a share of threatened species, but most animals on display belong to species that aren't threatened and will never be reintroduced (see I12).

text.bold: 4. Breeding for conservation doesn't require display.

paragraph.text: Programs that work usually involve specialized breeding centers, protected areas and planned releases. This can be done without turning the animals into an attraction.

Conservation programs look after the species, and not always after each animal's welfare: individuals deemed surplus have been killed in European zoos, such as the giraffe Marius in Copenhagen in 2014. For the guide, conservation matters as a means of protecting the lives of real sentient beings (see A10).

text.bold: 6. Returning animals to the wild doesn't guarantee a good life.

paragraph.text: Most animals in the wild don't live well: they spend their lives under threat of hunger, cold, disease, parasites and predators, and in most species almost all young die shortly after birth. So, from the individuals' point of view, increasing the number of animals in the wild isn't automatically a gain. Conservation that looks only at a species' numbers can ignore each animal's suffering (see N1 and N2).
Zoos keep a share of threatened species; captive breeding helped some species recover
The number of species was later revised to 13 of 68
The species moved from "Extinct in the Wild" to "Endangered" on the IUCN Red List in 2023
(d) The strongest counter-reply: without captivity, these species wouldn't exist
The most serious version says that for species that only survived in captivity there was no alternative, and that rejecting zoos would mean accepting extinction.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: It justifies breeding for conservation, not the zoo as an attraction.

paragraph.text: The cases cited depend on specific programs, not on displaying animals to the public.

text.bold: The most effective response is still habitat.

paragraph.text: Without protected areas there is nowhere to reintroduce to, and the species stays stuck in captivity.

text.bold: It's a controversial question among animal advocates.

paragraph.text: Some accept breeding programs aimed at reintroduction and at each individual's welfare, and some reject all captivity. What doesn't hold up is using a few success stories to justify zoos in general.

The question is whether saving a species justifies keeping animals confined for display. When captive breeding is the only way to prevent an extinction, and is done with the aim of returning animals to the wild and with each one's welfare in mind, the discussion is legitimate. But that describes a small part of what zoos do.

The principle being tested is: "if some institutions helped save species, keeping animals in captivity is justified".
They're what the argument really defends

It's true that species like the Arabian oryx, Przewalski's horse, the California condor and the scimitar-horned oryx only exist in the wild today because there were individuals in captivity, and that captive breeding can be the last barrier against an extinction.
But these cases are few, almost always depend on habitat protection, and don't justify keeping animals on display in zoos in general.
